title: The best Android phones of 2026: 40+ tested and compared!
text:
## Google Pixel 10a: The best Android phone under $500

Google Pixel 10a

Flush camera design • Good performance and battery life • Strong cameras • Great software support promise • Excellent price

MSRP: $499.99

Google's best AI features, in a more affordable mid-tier device

Google Pixel 10a is a refined mid-range phone built around Tensor G4, a brighter 120Hz 6.3-inch display, tougher Gorilla Glass 7i, satellite SOS, and trickled-down Pixel AI features — paired with a reliable dual-camera system, 30W charging, and seven years of updates.

- Completely flush rear camera
- Smooth day-to-day performance
- Very reliable cameras
- Great battery life
- Google's Pixel software
- $500 price is sweeter than ever

- No built-in magnets
- Missing some more advanced Pixel features
- Almost identical to the Pixel 9a

Google nearly perfected the $500 smartphone with the Pixel 9a, so rather than reinvent it, the Pixel 10a refines it. The result is the easiest recommendation on this list. The specs that matter most are carried over intact: a capable 48MP primary camera that punches well above its price point, a 5,100mAh battery that handles genuinely grueling days without complaint, and the cleanest Android software experience you can get at any price. What’s new is subtle but meaningful. A completely flush rear camera, symmetrical bezels, Gorilla Glass 7i, a brighter 3,000-nit display, faster 30W wired charging, and Satellite SOS support. None of it is flashy, but all of it makes a good phone better, and Google managed to do it without touching the $499 price tag.

The camera system won’t win any spec sheet arguments. There’s no telephoto lens, and the 8x maximum zoom is purely digital. But in practice, it’s one of the best dual-camera setups at this price. Low-light performance is genuinely impressive, Night Sight does heavy lifting in dimly lit environments, and Google’s computational photography keeps colors and details looking natural across the board. The Pixel 10a also handles tricky subjects well, picking out fine details and fast-moving subjects with the kind of consistency you’d normally expect from a phone that costs significantly more.

The best thing Google did with the Pixel 10a was keep the price at $499.

The Tensor G4 chipset is a year old at this point, and 8GB of RAM means a handful of Google’s more advanced features are off the table. No Pixel Screenshots, no Magic Cue. But for everyday use the Pixel 10a runs smoothly and without frustration, and what you do get is a genuinely full Pixel experience: Now Playing, Google’s calling tools, Material 3 Expressive UI, and seven years of OS and security updates. At $500, no other Android phone comes close to bundling this much software quality, this much camera capability, and this much long-term reliability into one package.

## Motorola Moto G Power (2026): The best Android phone under $300

Motorola Moto G Power (2026)

8GB of RAM • IP68 and IP69 durability • Vegan leather finish

MSRP: $299.99

Motorola's Moto G Power (2026) is the brand's most complete budget phone right now.

The Motorola Moto G Power (2026) is the best cheap Motorola phone to buy right now, combining decent materials with solid IP protection and a dual-camera setup that actually works in day-to-day life. We'd still like to see longer update support, but the Pantone colors and goodies like a headphone jack and expandable storage make life better.

- Decent ultrawide camera
- Excellent IP rating and durability
- Clean Pantone colors
- Solid battery life

- Limited software support
- Outdated chipset
- Odd camera bump design
- Removed wireless charging

Motorola’s budget lineup has a bit of an identity problem right now with too many phones that look and feel alike, spread across too narrow a price range. The Moto G Power (2026) sits at the top of that pile at $299.99, and while it doesn’t dramatically distance itself from its cheaper siblings, it does enough of the right things to justify its place as Motorola’s best affordable Android phone. Dual IP68 and IP69 water resistance, a Gorilla Glass 7i display, a genuine ultrawide camera, and a 5,200mAh battery that pushes comfortably into a second day — that’s a more complete package than most phones at this price bother to offer.

...

It trails the Nothing Phone 3a and Samsung Galaxy A26 5G in both CPU and GPU tests, and matches its cheaper Moto G siblings more closely than you’d hope. Real-world performance is serviceable rather than smooth, handling everyday tasks well enough but showing its limits if you push it. The two-year Android update commitment is the other soft spot, and it’s hard to overlook when Samsung offers four years on phones that cost less. Where Motorola does stand out is the camera setup. The 50MP primary sensor with its f/1.8 aperture handles daylight shots with solid color accuracy, and the 8MP ultrawide is a meaningful step up over the macro-only lens on cheaper Moto G models. Low-light results are modest but honest, and the software macro mode consistently surprises. For $299.99, it’s not a perfect phone, but it covers the bases that matter most.

...

## Samsung Galaxy A17 5G: The best Android phone under $200

Samsung Galaxy A16 5G

MSRP: $199.99

Budget phone, flagship support.

The Galaxy A16 5G continues Samsung's trend of reliable budget phones, only this time it's equipped with flagship-grade software support that will see it enjoy up to six years of updates.

Positives

- Stellar software update promise
- Solid primary camera
- Decent battery life
- Great price
- Good charging

Cons

- Just-okay build quality
- Aging performance
- Weak peripheral cameras
- Bland design

At $200, the Samsung Galaxy A17 5G has one job: be the most sensible cheap Android phone you can buy. It mostly succeeds, and it does so on the back of a genuinely sharp 6.7-inch Super AMOLED display with Gorilla Glass Victus protection, a clean One UI experience, and six years of OS and security updates. No other brand at this price comes close to that kind of long-term commitment. The pill-shaped camera cluster and Key Island fingerprint sensor give it more visual personality than you’d expect for $200, and Samsung’s AMOLED panel still punches harder than the LCD alternatives in this tier when it comes to contrast and color depth.

...

Six years of updates and a stunning AMOLED display make the Galaxy A17 5G the easiest long-term bet at $200.

The 50MP primary sensor with OIS is the clear camera highlight, reliable in good light and decent enough when things get darker. The 5MP ultrawide and 2MP macro sensors are functional at best, and you’ll know it when you use them. The 5,000mAh battery is the other genuine bright spot, outlasting most of its competition in testing and hanging on well through light-to-moderate days. For anyone who needs a dependable, well-supported daily driver on a tight budget and isn’t planning to push the phone hard, the Galaxy A17 5G makes a reasonable case for itself. Just go in with realistic expectations about what $200 actually buys you.

text:
### Android Central Verdict 

The Tecno Canon 50 Ultra may cost less than $600, but that price shouldn't fool you. The phone performs quite well and comes with a set of impressive cameras. There's an extensive suite of AI features available and battery life that will last all day and then some. If you're in a country that sells the Canon 50 Ultra, consider yourself lucky.

...

The Camon 50 Ultra also integrates many of its AI features into the camera app, and I feel like this is where Tecno takes things a step further than Samsung. Instead of waiting until after I capture an image to add any AI flair, I can enable Auto Zoom directly in the viewfinder or swipe to the AI Art Studio to preview how an image would look in a specific style before I capture it.

FlashSnap is one of the camera features I can see myself using quite often if I had a pet or kids, as it uses a high-speed shutter to capture 15 frames per second and uses AI to select the clearest image of the lot. It's insanely good at capturing fast-moving objects, much better than I've seen from other manufacturers.

...

But beyond the extra modes and features, the regular camera experience is surprisingly adequate. Photos taken during the day are quite good, and while some AI enhancements occur in the background, it does a good job of cleaning up the images and balancing the lighting. This is also the case at night, where the camera does a decent job reducing noise and retaining quite a bit of detail.

Tecno also highlights the capabilities of the 3x telephoto zoom lens, which supports up to 60x digital zoom. The results aren't too bad at various zoom levels up to 10x, although things can start to look a little muddy at 20x. Still, the AI does a good job of cleaning things up at this level and even makes 60x-zoom images legible, though AI upscaling appears to do quite a bit of heavy lifting, especially when text is involved.

Still, for a phone under $600, I'm quite pleased with the quality of images.

...

Fortunately, I couldn't find many downsides to the Camon 50 Ultra. It's a sleek phone with incredible battery life, great performance, and a solid trio of cameras. It's a phone that's all about choice and making AI accessible to the masses. Instead of spending $1,300 on a Galaxy S26 Ultra, for example, you can spend less than half that on this mid-range doppleganger, and you wouldn't miss a beat.

Just as before, though, Apple’s kept just a single camera on the back — which is unheard of in an era where practically everything has a dual-camera setup. But despite this shortcoming, the iPhone 17e’s 48MP main camera performs brilliantly across challenging lighting conditions. From the sharp details and definition it pulls out, to how it neutralizes hotspots in bright scenes, it doesn’t disappoint. It’s also a master of low light, proving to me it’s the best camera phone of the bunch in terms of raw performance.

...

There’s good and bad with the Pixel 10a. Just like the iPhone 17e, the design makes it look like a generic slab — but at least Google’s made the camera housing completely flush and offers some fun color options. Despite these design tweaks, the phone is by and large similar to its predecessor, the Pixel 9a, including how it packs the same Tensor G4 chip as before.
Its 6.3-inch Actua display is surprisingly sharp and bright, besting its rivals with a peak brightness of 1,896 nits in our lab testing. Even better, it posted the longest battery life of the trio with an average of 15 hours and 16 minutes. Better yet, it also delivers the fastest wired charging times we’ve tested — reaching 64% in 30 minutes.

...

Even though the camera performance is better than most other mid-range phones, I’m disappointed that there's barely any improvement over its predecessor — a tougher pill to swallow now that its $100 price hike has pushed it to $599.
## Samsung Galaxy A57

...

Out of the bunch, the Samsung Galaxy A57 has the most premium look and feel — rivaling its flagship sibling, the Galaxy S26. Not only does it combine the glass-meets-metal build Samsung’s known to give its top-tier models, but it also manages to have an IP68 rating.
If you prefer a phone with a larger screen to see more of what you’re doing or stream your favorite shows while on the go, the Galaxy A57’s massive 6.7-inch Super AMOLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate doesn’t disappoint. It’s way bigger than the 6.1- and 6.3-inch screens of the iPhone 17e and Pixel 10a, respectively.
(Image credit: Tom's Guide / Stephen Lambrechts)
Another notable feature is how it’s the only phone in this trio to pack a triple-camera system on the back, pairing a 50MP main sensor with a 12MP ultrawide and a 5MP macro lens. While that dedicated macro shooter feels more like a forced addition just to give it the upper hand, having three distinct lenses nonetheless gives you extra shooting versatility that neither the iPhone 17e nor the Pixel 10a can match.
Throw in some S26-level Galaxy AI features — like access to object eraser and a voice transcription tool — and it has a robust toolset to help save you time. I also love how it caters to power users like myself, with the ability to run two apps side by side, which neither the iPhone 17e nor the Pixel 10a can do.

...

Where the Galaxy A57 stumbles, though, is under the hood. ... Worse yet, it doesn’t even have the luxury of wireless charging — a glaring omission, in my opinion, now that its $50 price hike has pushed the cost up to $599.

## iPhone 17e vs. Pixel 10a vs. Galaxy A57: Bottom line
(Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide)
If there’s one I’d buy with my own money, it has to be the Pixel 10a — with the iPhone 17e not too far behind it. That’s because Google’s mid-range phone checks off more of the boxes on my list than the other two.
All three phones got price hikes, but the Pixel 10a’s $599 price tag is easier to swallow than the iPhone 17e’s heftier $699 cost. And while the Galaxy A57 matches the Pixel’s price point, its weak processing performance combined with flat camera results aren’t enough to prove to me it offers better value at the same price.
Ultimately, the Google Pixel 10a is the mid-range phone I recommend. I can’t stress enough the value of its software package alone — and backed up by seven years’ worth of major Android and security updates, it’s undeniably the smartest long-term investment you can make in the mid-range market right now.

## 1. Samsung Galaxy S25 FE — Best Overall When Under $600

Samsung Galaxy S25 FE

The Samsung Galaxy S25 FE is the safest all-around choice in this group when you can find the unlocked version at or below the $600 mark.

That distinction matters. The S25 FE gives U.S. buyers something many mid-range phones cannot: a more complete flagship-style experience backed by Samsung's enormous U.S. support ecosystem. It has a polished AMOLED display, strong day-to-day performance, capable cameras, IP-rated durability, wireless charging, and One UI's mature software experience.

It is not the phone with the biggest battery or the highest charging wattage here. Instead, Samsung gets the important everyday details right.

The display is excellent for streaming, social media, reading, and gaming, while the software feels much more mature than what you get from many aggressive value-focused brands. Samsung's Knox security, carrier availability, repair network, and long-term software commitment also make the S25 FE easier to recommend to someone who plans to keep a phone for several years.

The biggest problem is price. The unlocked 128GB version can sit above the $600 threshold at U.S. retailers, so this becomes the overall winner specifically when a promotion or retailer discount brings it into the target budget.

Why it stands out: It offers the most complete combination of display quality, cameras, software, durability, features, and U.S. support in this group.

Where it falls short: It does not have the enormous battery or ultra-fast charging of some of the international phones below, and its unlocked U.S. price can exceed $600.

Best for: buyers who want a dependable all-round Android phone and plan to keep it for several years.

## 2. Motorola Edge 70 Pro+ 5G — Best Camera Hardware

Motorola Edge 70 Pro+ 5G

The Motorola Edge 70 Pro+ 5G is the more interesting option if camera hardware and a premium-looking design matter more than Samsung's broader ecosystem.

Its biggest attraction is the camera hardware. A triple-camera setup with a dedicated telephoto camera gives you more flexibility than the typical two-camera mid-range phone. A proper telephoto lens is especially useful for portraits, distant subjects, travel photography, and situations where digital zoom starts falling apart.

Motorola also puts considerable attention into the display and physical design. The high-refresh-rate panel feels fluid while scrolling and gaming, and the slim body makes the phone easier to handle than some of the enormous battery-focused devices in this price class.

The catch for U.S. shoppers is important: this particular Pro+ model should not be treated as equivalent to Motorola's officially sold U.S. Edge models. Import availability, carrier compatibility, warranty support, and regional software can vary.

That means it is an interesting phone from a hardware perspective, but it is not as straightforward a recommendation as an officially sold U.S. model.

Why it stands out: The camera hardware and premium design are much more ambitious than what you normally expect from this price category.

Where it falls short: U.S. availability and after-sales support are less straightforward than with Samsung, Google, Apple, or Motorola's official U.S. models.

Best for: enthusiasts who specifically want this camera-focused hardware and understand the trade-offs of regional availability.

Samsung Galaxy S25 FE

## Final Verdict

The Samsung Galaxy S25 FE is our overall pick when you can get the U.S. unlocked model for $600 or less.

It does not have the largest battery or the most outrageous charging specification, but those numbers are not what make a phone great to live with. The S25 FE offers a much more complete combination of display quality, cameras, performance, software, durability, ecosystem support, and everyday reliability.

The Nothing Phone (4a) Pro is a very good alternative, but it is not the overall winner. Its design and software are genuinely different, and its U.S. availability makes it considerably more practical than several international phones in this list. Still, its appeal is more specific than Samsung's.
